XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: 5. A wnaiff y Gweinidog Cabinet roi diweddariad ar y cynnydd tuag at gyrraedd targedau natur a bioamrywiaeth Llywodraeth Cymru? OQ64581
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 5. Will the Cabinet Minister provide an update on progress towards reaching the Welsh Government's nature and biodiversity targets? OQ64581

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: We are making good progress in developing ambitious, legally binding biodiversity targets, which we must have in place by April 2028. The targets will be informed by expert and stakeholder advice, underpinned by robust evidence and impact assessment, and supported by delivery of our climate and nature action plan.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Diolch. On 2 June, when I raised this in the Siambr, the First Minister said that the Government is committed to clear public reporting on Wales's progress towards net zero through an accessible online dashboard. I went to have a look for it when some of the other dashboards came out, and all I could find was an old PowerPoint presentation about public sector emissions. Maybe I'm looking in the wrong place. Progress and opportunity for climate resilience is inextricably linked with the need to halt and reverse the loss of nature. I'm glad to see this recognised with the announcement of the forthcoming climate and nature plan, but we need to be clear about how progress on both will be monitored and reported. You'll be aware of the importance of the forthcoming targets due to be introduced in accordance with the Environment (Principles, Governance and Biodiversity Targets) (Wales) Act 2026, yet presently we don't have targets or any clear means of Member oversight on progress. Could you confirm the timeline for the introduction of those biodiversity and nature targets and whether you intend to monitor and report on progress openly using one of those dashboards?

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Thank you for the question. I am committed, as I said, to setting those targets across all the priority areas, and that work has to be done, in law, by April 2028. So, we will do that. As I said, we will work with stakeholders to get that in place. An independent advisory panel is providing expert scrutiny and evidence-based advice to us, while the biodiversity targets task and finish group brings together stakeholders from key sectors to help make sure that those targets are ambitious but also practical and realistically deliverable. They are being developed within a complex social, economic and environmental system. I could bore you with the theory of change and cost-benefit analysis and all of the work that's happening, but they are critical tools to understand that pathway to delivery, to assess the likely impacts and benefits of different interventions and then to build that robust evidence base that we need to support targeted development, implementation and evaluation. I hear what the Member is saying about transparency. I would expect that we would be looking to do that. I will maybe ask my colleague the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution to write to you with an outline. But, certainly, we intend to do that with other metrics across Government, and I can't imagine that it would not be the case here as well.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Last week, I asked the First Minister about the fact that NRW and other agencies do not know the full mix of chemicals discharged legally into the rivers of Carmarthenshire. A report has said that NRW are flying blind. As I wasn't quite sure of the response from the Cabinet Minister, I will ask the Cabinet Minister this: if we do not know exactly what chemicals are discharged into the rivers and how they interact with each other, how can we know what impact they are having on river ecosystems? How can we say with any confidence that this cocktail of pollutants isn't disrupting fish migration, harming fish and aquatic plants, and irreparably affecting river diversity? Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Thank you. I meet regularly with Natural Resources Wales. This is something that I will raise with them. Clearly, I have confidence in their ability to do their job, but I also recognise that they are being stretched and there is great demand on the expertise that they have. But I will pursue that with them and ask for an explanation.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: I welcome your rapid first steps on the climate and nature action plan for Wales, because if we're going to meet net zero by 2040 and achieve substantial nature recovery by 2050, we'll need to keep moving quickly and effectively, because the pace at which nature is declining in recent years is truly alarming. Since before the election, I've been in touch with groups like Save the River Usk, who are not just bringing much-needed attention to the subject but also building up detailed data sets at a grass-roots level, providing crucial local insights about the impact of the climate and nature crisis. You've said that the Government's new climate and nature board will reflect the experiences and priorities of people and communities across Wales. Will there be a role for informed and organised groups, like Save the River Usk, on the board so that their local knowledge and experience can be harnessed? Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: I will happily take that away and consider it. I think you make a fair point. I think the role of citizens—. And I said earlier, in relation to green spaces, when you empower citizens to take action and to respond to some of these circumstances, then you are really creating a more sustainable approach, moving forward. Citizen science, as well, I think, has a role to play. So, we'll consider all of that in the mix, and it's certainly something I can take on board. It's a point very well made.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Cynaliadwyedd Niferoedd Da Byw
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Sustainability of Livestock Numbers

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: 6. Pa asesiad mae'r Llywodraeth wedi'i wneud o gynaliadwyedd niferoedd da byw yng Nghymru? OQ64573
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 6. What assessment has the Government made of the sustainability of livestock numbers in Wales? OQ64573

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Well, the Government monitors livestock numbers alongside evidence on farm viability, on emissions, on biodiversity and on animal health, including through the UK Agriculture Market Monitoring Group. Our aim, of course, is to support sustainable, productive farming, and the sustainable farming scheme, for example, will help farmers improve resilience, strengthen food production and, of course, environmental outcomes at the same time.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Thank you. My colleague Laura Anne Jones mentioned back in July that Westminster's Climate Change Committee recommended a 25 per cent reduction in livestock numbers by 2040 in order to hit net-zero targets. Now, you've stated that there are no plans for a reduction, and that is something that I welcome, but it raises a further question to me, and it's one that's been discussed in this Chamber today. Given your dual role as Minister for rural resilience and sustainability, in scenarios where the interests of our rural communities stand in direct contrast with actions necessitated by net-zero policy, will you choose to back our farmers or bow to the interests of the climate lobby?

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: I think this is where Reform gets it wrong. You see it as one side against another. I would much rather find a way where we can mutually support both farming, by making it more resilient, but, in doing so, support the recovery of nature and tackling climate change as well. It isn't an either/or. I believe that we can—. And look, farming needs to become resilient. Nobody knows more than farmers the impact of climate change. They are the ones who are in the face of drought over the summer. They are the ones whose land sits under floodwaters for weeks on end. That has a direct impact on the economic bottom line. Many of the farmers I work with are the first ones to say, ‘We need to stop this flooding happening. We need support from Government and others to develop some of these interventions. Not only will it help nature and the environment, but, by damn, it will make our business more sustainable moving forward.' So, that is my approach, not this 'let's go and look for a fight' approach that we get from Reform.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Gwydnwch Gwledig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Rural Resilience

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: 7. Sut mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn hyrwyddo gwydnwch gwledig yng Nghasnewydd Islwyn? OQ64590
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 7. How is the Welsh Government promoting rural resilience in Casnewydd Islwyn? OQ64590

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Well, we are, I can assure the Member. We are strengthening rural resilience, Dirprwy Lywydd, across all rural Wales through investment in sustainable farming, in support for rural communities and businesses, actions to improve climate resilience, and new proposals for our rural-proofing duty, to make sure that the needs of rural areas are considered, of course, when developing policy programmes and spending plans as well.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Diolch yn fawr am yr ateb yna, a dwi'n falch eich bod chi yn gwneud yr holl waith yna hefyd.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Thank you very much for that response, and I'm pleased that you are doing all of that work.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: I want to turn to a specific issue that I've raised with you in the past, the water pressure in Redwick. The residents of this village, just outside Newport, have suffered with low water pressure for many years due to inadequate water infrastructure serving their community. This problem is exacerbated during periods of dry weather, like the unprecedented one that we have just experienced. There are five farms in the area and the water supply problem is so bad that some farms are unable to adequately supply their dairy herds. The water supply is so low it cannot keep up with the thirst of the animals. So-called mitigation measures have been put in place, but they have fallen short, and, in some cases, failed to materialise. The only solution to this is upgrading the flow of water into the village through major infrastructure overhaul. Minister, what pressure can you bring to bear on the situation and, in particular, Dŵr Cymru, to make this happen? And what action would you expect to happen before next summer so that we don't see the same problems happening again?

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Well, thank you for raising this issue again, in fairness. I share your concern about the problem with water pressure in Redwick and, as I say, it's something that you've raised previously. It is vitally important, first of all, of course, that people have a reliable water supply, but it's also important that farms and other businesses have the water that they need, and animal health and welfare considerations as well are essential, aren't they? So, my understanding is that Dŵr Cymru is investigating the situation and plans to update Redwick residents in October, but it is important that they assess the situation thoroughly and that the problem is addressed. This may, of course, need stages of action. There may well be short-term initial steps that they can take, but then there may be longer term requirements to plan and then implement schemes, and that will depend, of course, on what exactly the problem is and what exactly the best solution might be. But I will commit to raising this with Dŵr Cymru. I meet with them quite regularly, as it happens, and this is something that I will ask them about when we next meet.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: A'r cwestiwn olaf i chi, Weinidog, cwestiwn 8. Adrian Mason.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: And the final question to you, Minister, question 8. Adrian Mason.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Unigrwydd Cymdeithasol mewn Cymunedau Ffermio
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Social Isolation in Farming Communities

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: 8. Beth mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei wneud i fynd i'r afael ag unigrwydd cymdeithasol mewn cymunedau ffermio yng Nghlwyd? OQ64571
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 8. What is the Welsh Government doing to tackle social isolation in farming communities in Clwyd? OQ64571

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Well, the Welsh Government is tackling social isolation in farming communities through its national connected communities strategy. We also support farming communities through the Wales farm support group, which brings charities together to share expertise to provide practical and well-being support.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Diolch, Minister. Farming can be a lonely occupation. Long hours, financial pressures and geographical isolation can place enormous strain on farmers—and their families, of course. We know that poor mental health and suicide are serious concerns for farming communities, yet those most in need of support are often the least likely to seek it. You and I both represent Clwyd, and we know how important farming is to our communities, but, behind the farm gates, there can be individuals struggling in silence, often with nobody to turn to. What specific steps is the Welsh Government taking to identify farmers who are struggling, ensuring that mental health support goes even to the most isolated communities, and intervening before developing into a crisis? And crucially, Minister, how are we ensuring our support reaches the people who need it most, not simply waiting for a farmer in despair to find the courage they need to ask for help?

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Yes, improving mental health and well-being is an absolute priority for Welsh Government. We know that farmers face many challenges. I myself have seen it in terms of friends and family in the industry. That uncertainty that comes, of course, with so many aspects of farming, but the isolation and the loneliness particularly that you point to, can have a detrimental impact on mental well-being.

So, officials are working with local authority information and advice assistance services to identify people experiencing loneliness or isolation earlier, or as soon as we can, to try and connect them then to the support that will help them. The sustainable social services grant from the Government funds third sector projects that help people stay connected and active locally, including befriending, social activities and outreach for those at risk of loneliness in rural and farming communities. And the Welsh Government supports Farmwell Wales as well, an online hub offering farmers and their families accessible advice on personal as well as business resilience, including on isolation and loneliness, and we know, of course, that a lot of good work is being done by farming charities out there, and I, and I'm sure other Members of this Senedd, would want to pay testament to the work that they do. It is essential that we do everything we can to raise awareness of the importance of maintaining mental and physical health, and, if somebody is struggling, and I can speak from personal experience here: talk to someone. Share the load; talk to someone. That's how you start getting better. Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 2. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Diolch yn fawr iawn i chi, Weinidog Cabinet.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Thank you very much, Cabinet Minister.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Symudwn ymlaen i eitem 3, cwestiynau amserol. Mae dau gwestiwn heddiw. Yn gyntaf, Huw Thomas.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: We'll move now to item 3, the topical questions. There are two questions this afternoon. The first is from Huw Thomas.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Colledion Swyddi Arfaethedig yn Admiral a Legal & General
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Proposed Job Losses at Admiral and Legal & General

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: 1. A wnaiff y Gweinidog y Cabinet ddatganiad am y colledion swyddi arfaethedig yn Admiral a Legal and General? TQ1493
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 1. Will the Cabinet Minister make a statement about proposed job losses at Admiral and Legal and General? TQ1493

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Member_job_title_English: Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Member_job_title_Welsh: Y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Fenter, Cysylltedd ac Ynni
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: It's disappointing to hear that Admiral and Legal & General are making redundancies that could impact the Welsh workforce, and today's announcement in relation to Greggs and its plans to shut factories and the proposals that may also impact manufacturing operations at its Treforest site in Wales are concerning, as is the news in relation to the reported closure of Subzero as well. Our priority in all of these cases is supporting workers who may be affected by these proposed redundancies. We're engaging directly with the companies and workforce representatives to ensure employees have access to the information, advice and employment support that they need.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Weinidog. As you can imagine, last week's announcements have caused huge anxiety for workers at both Admiral and Legal & General. These are well-paid jobs in an industry that's been a success story for Cardiff and south Wales over recent decades. The news not only impacts the workers at these companies, but also, more broadly, the Cardiff economy in the city centre. And, as I said, the financial services sector has been a huge success story for Cardiff, with Admiral growing from next to nothing to being Wales's only FTSE 100 headquartered company, and Legal & General being at the heart of the city centre's redevelopment in recent years.

Last Friday, Minister, Shav Taj and I, along with Cardiff's four Members of Parliament, met with the companies to press both companies to minimise compulsory redundancies and maximise redeployment opportunities. They need the Welsh Government on their side—the workers, the companies and the industry. So, Minister, have you been able to meet with the companies yet? Will you look to rapidly deploy ReAct and Careers Wales support, working with partners in the Department for Work and Pensions and local government? And, more widely, what support will the Welsh Government deploy to make sure that this industry can return to growth as soon as possible?

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Thank you to the Member. I'm meeting with Admiral UK Insurance's chief executive officer tomorrow and I'll be meeting with senior representatives of Legal & General, and we've also reached out to arrange meetings with the unions and workforce representatives. We don't know currently how these redundancies will be apportioned across the individual sites, and I'll be seeking clarity in both of those meetings on that subject with both companies. And we'll be, obviously, working with the companies to understand how they intend to support the affected workers, what we can do more generally to work with the companies and with the workforce to ensure that we continue to support their contribution to the Welsh economy and to the communities in which they're based. And we'll work constructively, obviously, with companies and unions and delivery partners once we know exactly what the position is in relation to the job losses and how we can most usefully help the workers concerned.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: I've been hearing from constituents who are concerned about the job losses at Admiral and Legal & General, and I know my colleagues both in Gŵyr Abertawe and Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd have also shared concerns with me about the impact these jobs will have not only on people in Cardiff, but also in Swansea and the local economies. Workers need certainty about their futures and how they're going to support their families and pay ever-increasing bills and rent. And, given the uncertainty around who will be impacted currently by these job cuts, I wonder if the Welsh Government could provide some certainty about what support can be offered to impacted workers.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Yes, certainly. We hold right at the forefront of our minds the very difficult position that many employees and families will be in at the moment, and we will be doing everything that we can to support them in every way possible. And once we have a clearer picture in terms of the potential impact, then, obviously, we can both structure our response, but also share information appropriately with the Senedd.

As I said, both these companies continue to be very important employers and we will also want to talk with them, both as individual companies, but also as representatives of important sectors, about how we can work positively with them to continue to sustain, maintain and, hopefully, grow their workforce in other areas of their activity. And once we have more information in relation to this, then, obviously, we'll share it with the Senedd.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Minister, hundreds of jobs are at risk between Admiral and Legal & General. This is devastating news for the entire Welsh economy, but especially for those who are losing their livelihoods. While artificial intelligence was not the sole reason for these job cuts, those losses are a sign of what's to come. Now, across the UK, businesses are cutting jobs, with a focus on becoming leaner and more efficient. Often, though, the use of artificial intelligence is the core behind those losses. Now, what conversations have you had with these companies about the role that AI has played in these job losses? What conversations have you had with other Ministers about creating a more futureproofed workforce that's safer from redundancies that AI that could cause to our economy? Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Thank you to the Member for his question. Yes, Admiral have said, in their reported comments in this case, that these changes, these workforce reductions, are not AI related. They relate to other factors. I'm not aware that Legal and General either have made the connection with AI, but have referred to wider restructuring across the whole of the group.

Nevertheless, obviously we as a Government are very conscious of the way in which artificial intelligence is both bringing opportunities—economic opportunities, for example—and driving the growth of our compound semiconductor cluster in Newport, and indeed across the wider region of south-east Wales, and are aware that there are risks as well, in terms of its impact upon particular sectors and particular categories of employment. We are monitoring, as a Government, the emerging evidence not just in Wales, but across the world, as to the interrelationship between artificial intelligence and the labour market, and particular sectors of it. I have had discussions only yesterday with other Ministers across Government about how we can best respond, both to maximise the opportunities that undoubtedly there are, but also the risks and challenges that come with the technology, and how we can prevent the downside while maintaining the opportunities that are available to us.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: The Llywydd (Huw Irranca-Davies) took the Chair.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Thanks to Huw for bringing this important issue up, and for Kiera for mentioning Gŵyr Abertawe. Thank you, both. Admiral's announcement that they were cutting 500 jobs has been devastating for our own communities in Gŵyr Abertawe, as Kiera mentioned as well, and we've had many e-mails about this. In fact, one came just in the time that we've been sitting here in Plenary. It's an important issue for the people of Swansea, because almost 2,000 people are employed by Admiral in the Swansea area. Admiral, of course, being Wales's only FTSE 100 company, recorded a £958 million profit last year, and it is my view, and the view of my fellow MSs, that these lay-offs are completely optional. This is causing concern, as we can imagine, because the economic situation of our own constituency is fragile, to say the most favourable thing, really.

So, can the Minister, please, after his engagement with the company, update both us from Plaid Cymru, but also people from other parties as well, on the situation, so that we can properly communicate with our constituents, because they are very, very concerned, and it has a disproportionate hit on the economy of Gŵyr Abertawe? Diolch yn fawr.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Yes, I think the Member makes a very, very important point, that these companies are such significant employers, of course, that they employ constituents right across the wider south Wales region. Certainly, once we are able to understand more of what the impact will be in relation to the workforce, then I will be keen to share that information, particularly with Members that have large numbers of constituents that were employed in both cases.

It's important to reiterate that these companies, but also these sectors, are important elements in the economy. While we are keen to understand in more depth the reasons for these particular proposals, we want to work with the companies, and with the sectors involved, in order to grow valuable employment in these areas, and that will also form an important part of our engagement with the companies involved.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: 2. Pa asesiad y mae Llywodraeth Cymru wedi'i wneud o effaith economaidd cynnydd sylweddol mewn prisiau tanwydd? TQ1502
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 2. What assessment has the Welsh Government made of the economic impact of significant fuel price increases? TQ1502

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: The escalation of the middle east conflict in early 2026 continues to impact on households and businesses in Wales. While the issue of fuel pricing is non-devolved, we are working closely with the UK Government and our various delivery bodies to provide advice and support to customers, and to respond to any inappropriate price rises.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Diolch am eich ymateb, Weinidog.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Thank you for your response, Minister.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
The issue is, of course, global in nature, but the impact is very much being felt locally. The price of fuel, especially diesel, is approaching an all-time high, and is already the most expensive anywhere in Europe at just under £2 per litre in many areas, but well over that in others, and there appears to be no end in sight. Welsh hauliers are reporting that this is adding many tens of thousands of pounds to their weekly fuel bills. Bus operators are reporting an increase in their fuel prices of 50 to 60 per cent since January this year. These costs cannot be absorbed indefinitely, and will eventually feed through into inflationary pressures.

Throughout my constituency, many are forced to commute by car. It isn't a decision my constituents get to make, they have to drive, and they will be hit very hard by this, not only at the pumps, but in those goods and services they purchase that rely on logistics. Gweinidog, you've mentioned work with the UK Government, but given the potential impact on household incomes, inflationary pressures and economic activity across Wales, could you tell us in more detail what those discussions have been like, when they've taken place with our UK Government counterparts, and whether any assessments have been made as to the projected duration of this spike in fuel prices? I'd also be keen to know, depending on the forecast, whether any measures will need to be taken to protect households and businesses from these escalating costs. Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I'm grateful to the Member for raising this very important issue, which, as I said earlier, has been an issue, sadly, since the beginning of the year, has at various times worsened, and we are going through a period of great concern, particularly in relation to the issue of diesel prices, as she suggests.

Fuel pricing is reserved to Westminster, and there's an important role for the UK Government here, and also the Competition and Markets Authority. I have raised the issue of fuel resilience, pricing and UK Government support with the UK energy Minister at a recent inter-ministerial meeting. I've called for appropriate UK Government support in situations where prices are escalating, and that remains our fundamental position.

We recognise the impact that road fuel price increases are having on household budgets, particularly, of course, when it's combined with the high cost of heating oil and the significant increases expected in the domestic energy price cap in January.

The Welsh Government recognises also that the sustained high fuel costs have consequences right across the Welsh economy. She mentioned the haulage sector and my colleague the Deputy Minister for Transport meets regularly with the haulage sector, has already discussed this issue earlier this year, and will continue to monitor the impact on that particular sector. It isn't, of course, limited to that sector. I'm conscious as well of the impact on bus operators, and I know that the Deputy Minister for Transport is meeting bus operators imminently, again to understand the particular problems that are arising now from the spike that the Member refers to.

Across the wider economy, of course, these increases, they raise operating costs, they raise distribution costs for all fuel-dependent sectors directly and indirectly. In all of our engagement, therefore, with the UK Government and other UK stakeholders, we will continue to raise these important matters, ensure that contingencies, where necessary, are put in place, and that the UK Government uses the full range of intervention tools and levers that they have—I'm particularly thinking now in the context of the budget—so that both businesses and hard-pressed households receive the support that is necessary at this difficult time.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Thank you to the Minister for the previous answer. I think a lot of what I'm about to say has been touched upon. We recognise that rising fuel prices are putting growing pressure on Welsh businesses, driving up the cost of deliveries, transport and everyday operations. For businesses already struggling with rising costs, Wales's 20 mph default limit adds further concerns about journey times and operating costs. Just days ago, a family-run haulage firm, CVH Transport Services in Caerphilly, went bust. Will you acknowledge the cumulative pressure these rising costs and Welsh Government policies are placing on Welsh businesses, and commit to working across the industry to ease the pain that these businesses are feeling? Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I'm grateful to the Member for his question. We are certainly very aware of the pressures in relation to the haulage sector and, as I said, we are engaging with the sector to make sure that we can support in the way that we can, but also that we can, in our representations to the UK Government, set out a very clear picture of the need for further intervention where necessary. We're maintaining regular engagement with the UK's fuel sector representatives and our UK Government counterparts to monitor prices, and we've made consistently clear to the UK Government the impact of higher fuel costs, particularly the pressures faced by fuel-dependent sectors like haulage. 

Road fuel pricing, as I said, fuel duty and market regulation are all reserved matters, but we've made clear to the UK Government the impact of sustained high prices on Welsh households and businesses, and we will continue to press for effective action by the UK Government through the levers available to it. We also support monitoring, as I mentioned, by the Competition and Markets Authority and the Fuel Finder scheme to strengthen transparency and competition, and we expect reductions in wholesale costs to be passed on promptly and fully where they are available.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Yn olaf, Janet Finch-Saunders
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Finally, Janet Finch-Saunders.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Minister, UK average petrol is now averaging around 173.5p per litre. In real terms now, I've seen it over £2 per litre—diesel that is—and north Wales is paying above the UK average. In terms of energy production, we have the Gwynt y Môr windfarm right off our coast, yet we have the highest fuel costs in north Wales. Minister, Wales is being hit from both directions: rising prices at the pump and an energy policy that leaves Britain increasingly dependent on imports. Higher fossil fuel prices are estimated to cost Welsh households, businesses and public services an additional £5.64 billion. In our rural communities, certainly in Bangor Conwy Môn, travelling by car is not a luxury but a necessity, particularly for our carers, farmers, healthcare workers and small businesses.

The previous UK Conservative Government froze fuel duty and cut it by 5p per litre. Conservatives then campaigned against its planned reversal, now that diesel is so extortionately high. At the same time, an industry taskforce reports that 25,000 UK oil and gas jobs have been lost since the general election, while UK energy import dependency stands at 43 per cent. Will you work with the UK Government to cut fuel duty, reverse its restrictions on new North sea oil and gas licences, protect skilled energy jobs, or will rural Wales once again be expected to pay more while Labour and Plaid Cymru prioritise ideology over the practical concerns? And I know that my colleague Andrew wishes to ask a question on the Veolia refinery.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Daeth y Dirprwy Lywydd (Kerry Ferguson) i’r Gadair.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: The Deputy Presiding Officer (Kerry Ferguson) took the Chair.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: [Inaudible.]

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Minister, the Veolia refinery in west Wales is classed by that company as a North American refinery for economic purposes. [Interruption.] Valero, sorry. If Trump brings forward his ban on diesel production coming over to the European market, and in particular the UK, have you had any conversations with Valero to understand what implications that would have for the refinery? Because that would have a devastating impact on the supply of diesel into the Welsh and UK market.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I met with Valero recently in Pembroke to have a wide-ranging discussion with them. They are an important employer in that region, and, indeed, through the supply chain, to Wales as a whole. They are one of only four remaining refineries across the UK, and they represent a critically important bit of critical national infrastructure. If we were not previously aware of that, we've certainly been made aware of that by the geopolitical insecurity of the last nine months. I certainly will speak with them. I'm sure they have been in regular touch with the UK Government in terms of the contingency planning that I've referred to, and we engage with the UK Government on that front as well. But I certainly will want to know what the latest position is. Of course, it's a complicated situation there, where they are also an important exporter to the US, and, actually, there would be a knock-on effect to US oil supplies. There are complicated reasons as to why that historically is true. So, it certainly is an important area, where we will be engaging with the UK Government and with Valero.

In relation to the broader points that Janet Finch-Saunders made, I think it certainly is an important factor that there is geographic variation across the UK in terms of fuel prices. There is some limited recognition through the UK Government of that in certain areas, but not to rural areas of Wales. I think that now is an important time to revisit that question in terms of equity and to see not just what the UK Government could do in terms of fuel prices in general, where it does need to act at this particular time, but also to recognise the particular impact in rural communities, which face even higher fuel prices than the average. We will certainly take those points forward in our discussions with the UK Government as well.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 3. Cwestiynau Amserol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 3. Topical Questions
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Diolch yn fawr iawn, Weinidog Cabinet.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Thank you very much, Cabinet Minister.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 4. 90-second Statements
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Symudwn ymlaen i eitem 4, datganiadau 90 eiliad. Laura Anne Jones.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 4. Datganiadau 90 eiliad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 4. 90-second Statements
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. A wonderful old school friend of mine and a constituent, Matthew Cox, was diagnosed in 2025 with motor neurone disease, a cruel terminal illness that progressively takes away the ability to move, speak, swallow and breathe. Faced with that devastating diagnosis, Matt has chosen to turn that negative into a positive and devote his energy to helping others with MND now and in the future. Matt's warmth and generosity has always been extraordinary; now, so has his determination.

He has chosen to complete a number of marathons to help reach his goal of £100,000—which you can follow on his Instagram, @matthewjamescox—driven by his want to give money to the charities that have supported him after his diagnosis, that have helped him when he's felt so lost. This included the MND Connect helpline, which was literally, I believe, a lifeline for him and many others facing this cruel disease. He completed the London, Leeds, Welsh and, recently, the Great North Run marathons, where he doubled the distance he walked every time, which is an incredible accomplishment.

My plea to this Government, and to this whole Senedd, is to help ensure that support is there for every family facing this devastating disease. Matt, you're giving others hope, and I'm proud to call you my friend.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 4. Datganiadau 90 eiliad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 4. 90-second Statements
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Yr wythnos diwethaf, cofnodwyd 100 mlynedd ers agor y Stiwt, neu Blas y Mwynwyr, yn Rhosllanerchrugog. Adeiladwyd y Stiwt gan y gymuned i'r gymuned. Rhwng 1924 a 1926, rhoddwyd ceiniog o bob tunnell o lo o’r pyllau lleol tuag at adeiladu'r theatr. Codwyd bron i £18,000, swm anferthol ar y pryd. Parhaodd y glowyr i gyfrannu, gan roi 2c o’u cyflogau wythnosol tuag at y cynnal a chadw. Agorwyd y Stiwt ym 1926, yr un flwyddyn â’r streic gyffredinol. Yng nghanol caledi enfawr ac ansicrwydd, gwnaeth glowyr y Rhos rywbeth anhygoel: lle ar gyfer adloniant, addysg, y gymuned a bywyd diwylliannol Cymreig. Ers cenedlaethau, mae wedi bod yn fynediad at y celfyddydau. Fel y dywedodd Mark Lewis Jones yr wythnos diwethaf, 'Fe ddechreuodd o i gyd yn y Stiwt'.

Pan gaeodd y Stiwt ym 1977, gallai’r cyfan wedi dod i ben, ond wnaeth y gymuned ddim caniatáu hynny. Ar ôl ymgyrch penderfynol a £2.1 miliwn o’r gronfa loteri treftadaeth, ailagorwyd y Stiwt ym 1999. Mae ein dyled yn fawr i bawb a ymgyrchodd i’w arbed. Nos Wener, cawsom noson anhygoel yn y Stiwt yn dathlu'r canmlwyddiant yng nghwmni talent rhyfeddol ar y llwyfan. Hefyd, roedd yn fraint y llynedd i gwrdd ag Emyr Prys Jones, crëwr ffenestr liw hyfryd y Stiwt, teyrnged pwerus i dreftadaeth ddiwydiannol y Rhos. Felly, efo’r Stiwt yn dathlu 100 mlynedd, gadewch i ni ddathlu nid yn unig yr adeilad ond y gymuned a’i adeiladodd, a'i achubodd, ac sy’n parhau i roi bywyd iddo.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Last week marked the hundredth anniversary of the opening of the Stiwt, or Plas y Mwynwyr, in Rhosllanerchrugog. The Stiwt was built by the community for the community. Between 1924 and 1926, a penny was donated for every tonne of coal mined from the local pits towards building the theatre. Almost £18,000 was raised, a huge sum at the time. The miners continued to contribute, giving 2p from their weekly wages towards maintenance. The Stiwt was opened in 1926, the same year as the general strike. Amid enormous hardship and uncertainty, the Rhos miners built an incredible thing: a place for entertainment, education, the community and Welsh cultural life. For generations, it has been a gateway to the arts. As Mark Lewis Jones said last week, 'It all started in the Stiwt'.

When the Stiwt closed in 1977, it could have all come to an end, but the community didn't allow that. After a determined campaign and £2.1 million from the heritage lottery fund, the Stiwt was reopened in 1999. We owe a great debt to all those who campaigned to save it. On Friday night, we had an amazing night at the Stiwt celebrating the centenary in the company of incredible talent on stage. It was also a privilege last year to meet Emyr Prys Jones, the creator of the Stiwt's beautiful stained glass window, a powerful tribute to the industrial heritage of the Rhos. So, with the Stiwt celebrating 100 years, let's celebrate not only the building but the community that built it, saved it, and continues to give it life.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 4. Datganiadau 90 eiliad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 4. 90-second Statements

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 4. Datganiadau 90 eiliad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 4. 90-second Statements
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Tomorrow marks International Day of Older Persons, a fitting occasion to pay tribute to the array of community centres and organisations across Afan Ogwr Rhondda, and indeed the whole of Wales, that do absolutely vital work supporting older people. Today, I want to focus particularly on overcoming isolation and loneliness, the hugely important but often overlooked social determinants of health for older people. There are many community organisations in Afan Ogwr Rhondda that do life-affirming work by bringing older people together with people of all ages. They help make sure that getting older does not mean becoming isolated. In Caerau, Noddfa community centre, run by Matthew Rowlands, is at the heart of the community, offering a dizzying array of activities from fitness classes to craft sessions. I'd be remiss not to mention the Caerau Men's Shed here as well, where Phil, Gyp and everyone involved there do brilliant work. Then over to Gwynfi Miners Community Hall, where Simon is doing an unbelievable job providing a space that genuinely makes people's lives better, with walk-and-talk groups, book clubs, a gym, and much more. There's Gilfach community centre, Pen Rhondda Support Group, Treorchy Senior Citizens Club, and Action for Elders in Aberavon. I've had the privilege of seeing first-hand and hearing about the difference all of these organisations make for older people in our communities, ensuring that everyone has the opportunity to live a long life while remaining connected to the people and places around them.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 4. Datganiadau 90 eiliad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 4. 90-second Statements
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Diolch iddyn nhw i gyd.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Thank you to them all.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 4. Datganiadau 90 eiliad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 4. 90-second Statements
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Yesterday marked World Heart Day, a day that brings together a global community to raise awareness of cardiovascular disease, one of the most significant health challenges we face. CVD is responsible for more than one in four deaths in Wales, and Public Health Wales projects a 46 per cent increase in heart failure by 2035. These figures are stark, and they remind us why continued action, investment and awareness are so essential. I want to extend my thanks to the British Heart Foundation for bringing the red bench to the Senedd steps yesterday. It served not only as a symbol of remembrance, but also as a powerful prompt for conversation about prevention, early diagnosis and support. I'm grateful to all Members who took the time to visit the bench and showed their commitment to improving heart health across our communities. I also want to place on record my appreciation for the many individuals, clinicians, researchers, volunteers and organisations across Wales who work tirelessly to prevent cardiovascular disease, improve care pathways and strengthen the data we rely on to deliver better outcomes. Their dedication ensures that no matter where people live in Wales they can access the support and treatment they need. Together, we can continue to raise awareness, promote healthier lifestyles, and push for the improvements that will save lives for generations to come.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 4. Datganiadau 90 eiliad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 4. 90-second Statements
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
As Childhood Cancer Awareness Month draws to a close, I want to recognise children and families who are living with, and whose lives have been turned upside down by, a cancer diagnosis. In Gŵyr Abertawe, Latch is supporting 15 children affected by cancer and their families. As a clinician, I recognise the importance of treatment and care, and as a mother, I think of parents sitting by the hospital bed, holding their child's hand, trying to offer reassurance while carrying fears of their own.

Behind every diagnosis is a child missing friends and school, and a family learning to live with uncertainty. I thank Latch for their emotional, practical and financial support, and for helping families stay close when they need each other most. I pay tribute to the NHS teams, volunteers and fundraisers who bring care and comfort through difficult times.

We remember too the children who've died and their families, who carry their love and their loss every day. To every family facing childhood cancer, you deserve to be heard, understood and supported. September may be ending, but our support must continue throughout the year. Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 5. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Tir halogedig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Cynnig NDM9302 Niamh Salkeld

Cefnogwyd gan Alun Cox, Andrew Griffin, Anthony Slaughter, Art Wright, Becca Martin, Elwyn Vaughan, Elyn Stephens, Jayne Bryant, John Davies, Kiera Marshall, Lis McLean, Lyn Ackerman, Matthew Jones, Paul Rock, Peredur Owen Griffiths, Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, Sera Evans, Vikki Howells

Cynnig bod y Senedd:

1. Yn nodi:

a) y gwaddol o dir a allai fod wedi’i halogi a adawyd gan orffennol diwydiannol Cymru, a all beri risgiau difrifol i iechyd pobl, iechyd anifeiliaid a’r amgylchedd ehangach;

b) bod llawer o’r tir hwn wedi’i halogi o ganlyniad i weithgarwch diwydiannol hanesyddol, a bod y baich o reoli atebolrwydd yn aml yn disgyn ar gymunedau lleol ac awdurdodau cyhoeddus;

c) nad oes darlun cenedlaethol clir na chyson o dir a allai fod wedi’i halogi ledled Cymru;

d) y pryder a'r ansicrwydd hirdymor y mae cymunedau sy’n byw ger y safleoedd hyn yn aml yn eu hwynebu;

e) pwysigrwydd yr egwyddor ‘y llygrwr sy’n talu’ o ran sicrhau bod y rhai sy’n gyfrifol yn cyfrannu at gostau adfer y tir.

2. Yn cydnabod y gwaith sydd eisoes wedi’i wneud gan awdurdodau lleol, Cyfoeth Naturiol Cymru a chyrff eraill i nodi tir halogedig, ymchwilio iddo a’i adfer.

3. Yn galw ar Lywodraeth Cymru i wneud y canlynol:

a) cydweithio â Llywodraeth y DU i sicrhau bod costau adfer yn cael eu talu gan y rhai sy’n gyfrifol am lygru;

b) galw ar Lywodraeth y DU i gyflwyno mecanwaith cyllido penodol i gefnogi’r gwaith o ymchwilio i dir halogedig a’i adfer, pan na ellir adennill y costau gan y rhai sy’n gyfrifol;

c) sefydlu fframwaith cenedlaethol ar gyfer profi ac asesu tir a allai fod wedi’i halogi, gan roi blaenoriaeth i’r safleoedd sy’n peri’r risgiau mwyaf; 

d) cefnogi awdurdodau lleol i gyflawni eu cyfrifoldebau statudol.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Motion NDM9302 Niamh Salkeld

Supported by Alun Cox, Andrew Griffin, Anthony Slaughter, Art Wright, Becca Martin, Elwyn Vaughan, Elyn Stephens, Jayne Bryant, John Davies, Kiera Marshall, Lis McLean, Lyn Ackerman, Matthew Jones, Paul Rock, Peredur Owen Griffiths, Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, Sera Evans, Vikki Howells

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Notes:

a) Wales's legacy of potentially contaminated land arising from its industrial past, which can pose severe risks to human health, animal health and the wider environment; 

b) that much of this land contamination is due to historic industrial activity, with the burden of managing liabilities often falling on local communities and public authorities; 

c) the absence of a clear or consistent national picture of potentially contaminated land across Wales; 

d) the long-term concern and uncertainty often experienced by communities living near these sites; and 

e) the importance of the ‘polluter pays’ principle in ensuring that those responsible contribute to the costs of addressing its remediation. 

2. Acknowledges the work already undertaken by local authorities, Natural Resources Wales, and other bodies to identify, investigate and remediate contaminated land.

3. Calls on the Welsh Government to: 

a) work together with the UK Government to ensure that the costs of remediation are borne by those responsible for polluting;  

b) call on the UK Government to introduce a dedicated funding mechanism to support the investigation and remediation of contaminated land, where costs cannot be recovered from those responsible; 

c) establish a national framework for the testing and assessment of potentially contaminated land, prioritising sites that pose the greatest risks; and 

d) support local authorities to fulfil their statutory responsibilities.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 5. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Tir halogedig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Firstly, I would like to thank all the Members who have shown their support for this debate today. I especially want to thank Elwyn Vaughan, who has worked closely with me on this motion and has been a strong advocate for change in his constituency as well. The fact that this motion has support from Members across the Senedd and from different parts of Wales is significant, because contaminated land is not an isolated or local problem. It's a legacy of our shared industrial past, which communities across Wales live with to this day. I look forward to hearing from Members in this debate, and particularly about the experiences of communities in their own constituencies.

For many people across Wales, our industrial past is not simply something confined to the history books. It's something that communities continue to live with today. We see that with our coal tips, which remain a visible part of the landscape in many of our communities. But the legacy of contaminated land is often much harder to see. Toxic substances left behind by historic industrial activity can remain in our ground for decades after that activity has ended, and in the case of some chemicals, they can be in our ground for generations.

So, what do we mean when we talk about contaminated land? As Natural Resources Wales explains, land can become contaminated through previous industrial, commercial or landfill uses, including where contamination has migrated from an adjacent site. That can include heavy metals, such as arsenic, cadmium and lead, oils and tars, solvents and gases, alongside radioactive substances. And those consequences can extend beyond the disposal site itself, with contamination potentially affecting human health, animal health and also our wider environment. We've also heard increasing public concerns about persistent chemicals, such as polychlorinated biphenyls, or PCBs—a group of toxic, human-made, hazardous chemicals that have dangerous effects on our environment and our health, which can remain in the environment for long periods of time.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 5. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Tir halogedig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
The recent BBC documentary Buried, presented by Michael Sheen, has brought renewed attention to this issue of contaminated land, which I very much welcome, and I would like to thank all of those who have been involved in its production. However, we must recognise that, for many communities, these concerns have been raised by them for many years. Campaigners and communities across Wales have been raising these issues with us, and quite a few of them are actually up there in the gallery today.

And I've seen the impact of that legacy first-hand in my own constituency. In Ynysddu, Ty Llwyd quarry was actually featured in the recent documentary, with the two Jans. It's a site where local people have been raising concerns for years about the historical disposal of chemical waste, its links to Monsanto's former manufacturing plant in Newport and what that legacy could mean for the surrounding community. There have also been concerns about leachate leaving the former quarry site, particularly following periods of heavy rainfall, and the potential for contaminants to move then into the surrounding area.

I want to take this opportunity to thank Councillor Janine Reid, who is here as well today, and also her colleague Councillor Jan Jones, for the tireless work that they have done to raise these concerns and make sure that their community's voice is heard.

But, ultimately, Ty Llwyd is about more than what is happening at a former quarry site. It's about the people who live alongside it. For those people, this is not an abstract environmental issue. It's something that's been hanging over the community for years. It's about the place where people live, where their children have grown up and where people go and walk their dogs. It's about being able to feel confident that the place they call home is safe and that their community and its future are being protected.

As Councillor Reid put it:

'For our community, Ty Llwyd is not an abstract environmental issue—it is something that has been hanging over us for years. The consequences of what has happened here are felt by the people who live alongside it.

'We need the contamination to be properly understood, the risks to our community to be taken seriously, and a clear plan to ensure that Ty Llwyd along with other sites in Wales, do not continue to be a source of concern for local people—with reassurance that our community and its future are being protected.'

And I think that quote from Janine gets to the real heart of this issue today. People shouldn't have to live for years with unanswered questions about what may be beneath their feet, what may be moving through the land around them, or what the potential risks could be. They deserve clear information about what is known, a proper understanding of the risks, and confidence that there is a clear plan in place on how we deal with those risks. And, as we know, Ty Llwyd is not unique. Across Wales, there are thousands of sites with a history of industrial or other potentially contaminating activity—from north to south, from Cefn Mawr to Maendy, communities across Wales are living alongside that legacy.

Research by Friends of the Earth Cymru has identified more than 45,000 potentially contaminated land sites across Wales. And while that gives us some indication of the scale of this issue, it also highlights the fact that we still do not have a clear national picture of potentially contaminated land across Wales. We need to know where these sites are, what contaminants may be present and which pose the greatest risks to our communities and to our environment. And that is why this motion today calls for a national framework for the testing and assessment of potentially contaminated land, prioritising those sites that pose the greatest risks. We need to know where these sites are. We need to understand what contamination may be present and the risks it poses. And we need to make sure that the sites presenting the greatest risks are prioritised.

But there is also another important issue here, and that is who pays. The principle of 'polluters pay' should be at the heart of this approach. Where the person or the company responsible for pollution can be identified and held responsible, they should contribute towards the costs of putting it right. That burden should not simply fall on our local authorities, and it shouldn't fall on the taxpayers either.

But. of course, as we know, with historical contamination it's not always straightforward. Some companies may no longer exist. Ownership may have changed. Records may be incomplete. That's why the motion also calls for the UK Government to introduce a dedicated funding mechanism for cases where the costs cannot be recovered, because there has to be a solution for those sites as well. We cannot have a situation where a local authority knows there is a potential problem, but does not have the resources to properly address it. And we cannot expect communities to carry the burden of historical industrial activity simply because the pollution happened many years ago.

Local authorities, Natural Resources Wales and other organisations are already doing important work in identifying, investigating and managing contaminated land. But they need the resources and the support to fulfil those responsibilities. And communities need confidence that, when they raise concerns, those concerns will be properly investigated.

So, Dirprwy Lywydd, this motion is ultimately about making sure that the legacy of our industrial past is managed properly and fairly. It's about having a clearer national picture of contaminated land. It's about prioritising the sites where the risks are greatest. It's about giving local authorities the support that they need. And it's about making sure that, where possible, those responsible for pollution contribute to the cost of putting it right.

The communities living alongside these sites did not create this contamination, so they should not be left with carrying the uncertainty, the potential risks or the costs. For those reasons, Dirprwy Lywydd, I hope Members across the Siambr will support this motion today. Diolch yn fawr.
