XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Diolch yn fawr iawn, Gwyn.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Terfyn cyflymder diofyn 20 mya
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I apologise for using the word 'blanket'. When it comes down to the policy itself, generally, which is not a blanket policy in any way, it's a good thing. And I will use data to illustrate this. As a lecturer in Swansea University I'm very used to PowerPoint presentations, and I think it is very strange to discuss data, especially graph-based data, where you can do with lines on graphs, and I don't have that luxury. I was going to ask Louise, she had a very nice paper-based graph, and I thought about adopting that, but then I thought I would never be able to draw the graphs or the pictures in anywhere near your style, for my writing is terrible. So, I'll use the actual figures instead, although they are more tedious to read out like this.

First of all, they come from Senedd research, because I thought everybody would respect that, and the UK Government's STATS19 road safety data, and I was going to separate this into four parts: collisions, injuries, economics, and the culture of it.

First of all, collisions. There's been a 22.5 per cent fall in collisions after the 20 mph limit was introduced in September 2023 and, on other roads, a 0.2 per cent fall. In England, this fell by 4.7 per cent, and in Scotland it went up by 1.5 per cent. That's collisions.

And then we come to injuries. Casualties, there have been 630 fewer casualties of all kinds. Deaths—it went down from over 100 to 84, but you're quite right in saying it went from 84 to 91, but this is still down from where it was before. An 11 per cent decrease in those killed or seriously injured.

And then there is the economics of it. Can you put a price on life? Well, yes, you can. That's the basis of healthcare economics as well in medicine, when you put a price on lives saved versus cost to the economy. And there is projected cost to the economy, you're quite right in saying that as well. Do they balance up? There's not enough data to come to a conclusion yet. But, and I won't read out these tedious figures, but there is: pounds for everybody killed, measured in the millions, mainly because of the way the road is closed, traffic is diverted and such; hundreds of thousands of pounds for somebody seriously injured; and some £20,000 for somebody slightly injured. And there's been many estimates as to what this adds up to, but, again, without the use of PowerPoint or a graph-based phenomenon,

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: I will take a leaf out of your book, and I'll say, 'Yes, I will welcome the intervention.'

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Terfyn cyflymder diofyn 20 mya
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: There's a thing called an opportunity cost: when you spend money on one thing, it means you're not spending money on another. If you accept that there are economic costs of the 20 mph default speed limit to the Welsh economy, and if you accept that the Welsh Government has spent £30 million-odd implementing the measure, and many millions more since reviewing the measure, how many lives could have been saved had that money been spent on our emergency departments, on beds in our hospitals, or on other matters like that? It's an interesting one to quantify, is it not?

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Terfyn cyflymder diofyn 20 mya
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: It's an interesting one, and I think it's a very legitimate point, opportunity costs. I would answer that by saying that we're in a situation now whereby I am told by the scientists that it will take until 2029 for them to have properly understood both the economic and the lives-saved cost of this, and we can't come to a proper decision as to what those costs would be, pro and con, until 2029. We have the option of finishing the experiment early and not knowing whether it would have made a difference one way or the other, or waiting until 2029. It might well be that, when that comes to an end, they say the drift upwards in casualties or lives might have continued, it might come back down again, but until we've reached that date—and that's a date chosen by people who are more intelligent than I—we can't know. So, the answer is, as a scientist, I will say that we can't know the answer to that question, because the time hasn't elapsed yet for us to properly compare the data. I'm aware the clock has gone red, but also I'm aware of the culture of this place—that if you accept an intervention, you get a little bit of grace.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Thank you. With regard to culture, to come back to that aspect, people used to play outside more. I went to Sketty Primary School in our constituency this week. One of the greatest problems is people being addicted to social media—not playing outside, but indoors. Max Boyce, when he used to sing about this four-hours-each-way match, 'When I Played for Wales'—Wales against England, it was something like 400-odd against 12—he played in Llewellyn Street in Glynneath. I've never been been to Llewellyn Street in Glynneath, but I encourage people, for preventative health, mental health, all that kind of thing, to be outside. Let's play outside more. Less social media. Less in the house. So, for multiple reasons, I think this is a good thing. Thank you. Diolch yn fawr.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Terfyn cyflymder diofyn 20 mya
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
It's a pleasure to be able to speak in this debate today, tabled in the name of my friend Llŷr Powell, on scrapping one of the most hated pieces of legislation to come out of this Chamber in a decade. A policy cooked up by Labour and Plaid Cymru, not in response to public demand, not with solid evidential basis, but because it was a fashionable left-wing policy that was gathering steam elsewhere, and they didn't want to lose out on the trend. The same can be said about the tourism tax, and now plans for rent control—all disastrous policies stolen from other failing far-left governments.

Nobody in this Chamber wants to see people killed or seriously injured on Welsh roads, and I think anybody who says that is disgraceful. The question is whether making 20 mph the default across thousands of miles of roads is the right way to achieve the objective of decreasing road traffic collisions. Three years after the policy came into force, we now have more evidence to examine. As Jason said, 91 people were killed on Welsh roads in 2025, 9 per cent higher than 2024. More significantly, Department for Transport figures from last year show the highest number of deaths on Welsh roads since 2019.

I'm aware that the increase in deaths was not necessarily on 20 mph roads, but the aim of an overall reduction in road traffic deaths has not been achieved. There is also a great deal of confusion. I regularly get stuck behind people going at 20 mph on roads with 30 mph or 40 mph limits. The confusion, I think, contributes to accidents. I literally had somebody last weekend on a 60 mph road going 20 mph. I overtook him, he put his hand on his horn and beeped me. I pulled up and I said, 'Are you okay?' And he said, 'No. Do you know this is 20 mph?' And I said, 'Mate, it's not.' And then we made friends and he was from outside the area. You can argue the details, but it's undeniable that this policy has failed in its overall objective and it has come at enormous cost to the Welsh economy. 

We also need an updated economic appraisal. We haven't had one since 2022, perhaps because the Welsh Government wouldn't like the results. But if they are confident in the policy, then let's see the data. Presiding Officer, this should never have been about ideology; it should have been about what actually works. If we want safer roads, let's target dangerous roads, improve road design and crack down on dangerous driving rather than imposing a blanket limit—[Interruption.]—across the entire country. I apologise—default. Let's end the anti-motorist agenda that punishes all road users. I urge all to vote with our motion to scrap this crazy failed scheme.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Terfyn cyflymder diofyn 20 mya
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Lywydd. The core of this debate appears to be a very simple question: do we accept the evidence that lower speeds save lives or do we not? Yes, this is about road safety, but it's also about value for money and it's about public health. Despite what some in this Siambr insist, the science tells us that the consequences of even small increases of speed are stark. At 30 mph, a pedestrian struck by a vehicle faces roughly a 50 per cent chance of suffering a severe injury; at 20 mph, that risk falls to 10 per cent. And let's be honest, even most of the loudest critics of the policy don't deny this. After all, they too usually want 20 mph limits outside schools, they are happy to have them outside hospitals and they think they're important around playgrounds and care homes. In other words, they acknowledge the principle. They accept that where vulnerable people are present, slower speeds save lives.

What strikes me about some of this debate is that it feels like the proposers of this motion are employing something I'm going to call 'imbyism'. They're quite happy to have that 20 mph speed limit outside their child's school, quite keen to have one outside the care home where their parents live, enthusiastic to have it on the road they cross every day. But what they're forgetting is that vulnerable people do not only exist within a few metres of a school gate or near a hospital entrance. Children need to walk to school from their homes, elderly people have to cross the road to get to the shops, disabled people need the freedom and confidence to travel around their communities. They need to navigate busy roads and residential streets every day. This is why the 20 mph policy was introduced—to reduce death and serious injury, to make people feel safer to walk and cycle around their communities, to reduce congestion and parking issues and to improve people's health, something I'm pleased had cross-party support in the previous Senedd.

When some people say that a 20 mph blanket ban—. Sorry. I do apologise. It's in my notes. I didn't mean to say it. It's really hard when I didn't realise. When some people say it infringes their freedom, they are ignoring the freedom of those people. The freedom—

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: That's very generous. Would you not agree with me that the reason why there's so few Labour people sitting on benches now—? This was one of the fundamental reasons why the people of Wales were so angry—that their petition of 0.5 million people was completely ignored. They were furious about the 20 mph policy. It has actually changed the Government here.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Terfyn cyflymder diofyn 20 mya
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Terfyn cyflymder diofyn 20 mya
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I couldn't possibly comment on that, except to point out that Plaid Cymru also support this, as do the Greens.

When some people say that the 20 mph default limit infringes their freedom, they're ignoring the freedom of those people—the freedom to walk safely in their communities, the freedom to cross the road without fear, the freedom to participate fully in community life. We need to be serious about encouraging a shift towards walking, wheeling and cycling, so we must create environments in which people feel safe to do so. We cannot talk about reducing congestion and parking issues whilst simultaneously arguing against measures that make streets safer for those who do not or are unable to drive.

That brings me to the practical alternative that is so often proposed: selective 20 mph zones for those schools, hospitals, care homes and playgrounds. Let's consider what that would mean in practice. The Welsh Government's nationwide implementation cost around £33 million. But if we were to scrap the 20 mph policy, which in itself would probably cost about £33 million again, and then redesignate every school, every care home, every hospital and every playground individually, at the average of £33,000 per location, the cost of that would be £163 million. I wonder whether Reform agree with me that £163 million is more money than £33 million. I understand that I can't use the B word in this debate, which is a shame, because communities need a simple, consistent layer of protection. The alternative, of course, is an expensive patchwork quilt of varying speed limits requiring more signs, more admin and more enforcement, leaving drivers confused as they try and work out which rule applies where. I'm nearly finished.

In this debate about cost, we're losing sight of the fact that lower speeds reduce the risk of death and serious injury. That's why the policy was introduced. That's why many opponents support 20 mph in the places they care about. That's why this debate ultimately comes down to this: whose freedom do we value in society? Is a car journey that is, on average, less than a minute quicker really more important than the ability of a child to walk safely to school, an older person to cross the road with confidence, or a disabled person to travel independently through their community? Almost one in five households in Wales do not have access to a car. Many of these people are old, disabled, young or poor. Why should they bear the consequences and the risk—

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Terfyn cyflymder diofyn 20 mya
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Diolch yn fawr iawn. We still have several speakers to get to. I do not think we will get to them all in a 60-minute debate. This is probably the final speaker here, before we go to the Minister and the concluding remarks. Carmelo Colasanto.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Terfyn cyflymder diofyn 20 mya
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Lywydd. I'm going to cover a lot of ground that's already been covered, but there are two separate questions in this debate, and too often they're deliberately rolled into one. The first is whether 20 mph is right in some places. Well, of course it is; we're not going to argue with you over that. Outside schools, around hospitals, on clearly defined residential streets where the evidence justifies it, nobody on these benches disputes that lower speeds make collisions less severe. The second question is very different: should 20 mph be the default for restricted roads—I'm not going to use that term—across Wales, with communities left to argue their way back to 30 mph?

This is where Reform takes a different and pragmatic view. The focus should be on realising the data isn't conclusive—and it hasn't even been properly evaluated yet—and actually focus on that, rather than taking the credit for an initiative that was really poorly executed. Trying to take the credit for a small dip is like me taking credit for Italy winning the world cup in 1982 because I switched my tv on once. It's absolutely preposterous. It's delusional. For me, I'd like to give my own perspective on why we've seen this dip, and it has nothing to do with the B word. We're all getting e-mails, all of us, from constituents regarding speeding on specific roads, in parks at night. I have it in my ward with regard to the A484, which is a racetrack. I have it in North Dock in Llanelli, I have it Llangennech in my ward.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Terfyn cyflymder diofyn 20 mya
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I have it in Llangennech in my ward. The most common factors, speaking to people and police officers for this behaviour and the change of behaviour, are as follows. Vehicles now have more safety measures than they ever did before—ever. There are fewer pedestrians around at night because they just don't go out because of the state of our roads. And these guys are speeding and driving at night. They do that because the police are spending less time patrolling in the evenings because of limited resources. So, there's another angle as to why you see that slight dip, and I think we're not looking at that.

There is a perception within people that lawlessness is acceptable, and the offenders that we should be focusing on take advantage of that. I'll give you an example of that perception, yes? On 5 March 2026, I witnessed a car overtake me in Felinfoel in a 20 mph zone at approximately 60 mph. The car was going so fast that he actually had to swerve into oncoming traffic and narrowly missed a pedestrian by 1.5 ft to 2.5 ft. I phoned the police on 999 and was told to stay on the line whilst I followed the car in traffic. The registration number was given. Fifteen minutes later, I was told they couldn't do anything because he'd crossed into another force area. That was 5 March. To date, as of this morning, that person has not been visited and spoken to. This is a guy who almost killed someone. So, I would suggest that, actually, we're looking in the wrong place.

Now, Reform believes in far, far stronger enforcement of measures. Target the problem. Don't put a default in there. It's absolutely preposterous. So, back to the default. So, what county decides whether you need your road to be a 20 mph zone? It isn't a school, hospital or a child's crossing. It's a lamppost because that's how we work our default out, by the space between the lights. So, if the street lights are close enough, it's 20 mph and it's up to your community to prove otherwise, which is a nonsense.

Now, as I said, collisions on 20 mph and 30 mph roads are dipping slightly and every one of us should welcome that. But they were already falling for around 10 years. This isn't an overnight thing. The post-policy period is short and the Government's evaluation isn't even finished. So, I would say: publish the evaluation in full. Show us which roads actually produced a benefit, because if the gains have actually come from streets where 20 mph was always the default, then that's wrong, isn't it? That's an argument for targeting, not a national default.

Then there is consent; 469,571 people signed a petition to say they didn't want this—iddn't want it. And we're accused of always talking Wales down, where it looks like they told you—500,000 people who didn't want it—and you talked them down. So, let's get our facts straight there. Transport for Wales' own monitoring sites in summer 2025 said that barely half of the vehicles are doing 24 mph or less. A default that half the drivers aren't keeping to has a credibility problem in itself. And when communities did push back, what happens? In Carmarthenshire, the council received 1,604 submissions from the general public. Hundred and fifty stretches of road were reviewed, and only 11 of those actually made it back to 30 mph.

Then the cost. The Government's own appraisal level predicted a net benefit. It estimated the cost of slower journeys at £6.35 billion over 30 years. And after counting every road safety, active travel and environmental benefit, its central estimate was still £-4.5 billion. Now to the Government. Plaid Cymru did not merely inherit this policy; you promised it and co-opted it. You promised it in your 2021 manifesto. You voted for it in 2022. Then this May, you asked for a mandate to govern without a word about the default in your manifesto.

At Reform, our manifesto is clear. Restore 30 mph as the default, keep 20 mph where it's generally needed outside schools and hospitals, and on clearly-defined residential streets, with a positive evidence-based case for each one. And invest in fixing dangerous junctions and collision black spots, instead of treating a change of science as a road safety strategy and a cash cow that you can milk.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Terfyn cyflymder diofyn 20 mya

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Terfyn cyflymder diofyn 20 mya
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Thank you. Evidence-led limits that improve safety without strangling town centres, and turning a daily commute into a daily irritation.

So, I ask the Deputy Minister for three things: publish the updated economic appraisal; give this Chamber firm dates for the evaluation, and commit to the Chamber today that if that comes back and it doesn't justify a national default, it goes. That's it—it goes.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Terfyn cyflymder diofyn 20 mya
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Firstly, just to set the tone, I wrote to all the business managers here this morning, and I copied the Llywydd in, to make sure that we were dealing with facts, so we had a factual representation. And I thank you, Vikki, for pointing to that in your contribution a few minutes ago. I was really disappointed early on to hear the 91 being repeated here. Let's just be clear that that isn't related to 91 deaths on 20 mph or 30 mph roads; that's across the piece. So, if we're going to talk about something that's related to 20 mph and 30 mph, like Vikki, I would like that to be explained when Jason wraps up.

The other thing I'd like to say is that the motion before us from Reform didn't make any of the caveats that have been referenced in the contributions from behind me, some of which have been worthwhile. We were clearly concerned, when we were in opposition in the last Senedd, to make sure that Labour in time dealt with this proposal in a different way, and I think even the Labour benches would probably agree that position now anyway. But it does concern me that we're continually going back over this old ground without dealing with the facts in front of us.

This Government is absolutely committed to reducing the number of people killed and seriously injured on Welsh roads. The responsibility for road safety is shared between all those who use the roads—those who design, regulate, manage and operate the transport system, and those who enforce its rules. We all have a part to play. This Government is clear that the 20 mph speed limit in areas where pedestrians and cyclists mix with motorised vehicles is fundamentally the right policy. The evidence so far points absolutely in the right direction. There are many fewer collisions and fewer people injured on these roads now. This supports the aim we should all share of no family having to grieve a loved one because of an avoidable tragedy.

It is important that this debate is grounded in evidence rather than assertion. Much has been said about the impact of 20 mph over the last three years, but the laws of physics are clear, and Gwyn referenced this earlier—I'm just building on that. A small increase in speed creates a much larger increase in collision energy. This means a car travelling at 30 mph carries 2.25 times more kinetic energy than the same car travelling at 20 mph. A vehicle at 30 mph needs almost twice the distance to stop as a vehicle at 20 mph. Driver reaction time increases from about 6m to 9m when comparing the two, meaning there is less time to perceive hazards. That is why, at 20 mph, collisions are more likely to be avoidable, and, if they occur, they are considerably more survivable than collisions at 30 mph. It is true that 91 people were killed in collisions in Wales in 2025, and one thing I'm really disappointed about in this debate is when we've talked about people's lives lost, I've heard laughter and derision from the benches behind me. This is a serious matter, and we'll hear this again and again and again. Seven more people than in 2024, but five fewer than the last calendar year before the introduction of the 20 mph default speed limit. Despite 84 and 91 fatalities in 2024 and 2025 respectively, there were only 19 fatalities on 20 mph roads. That is 19 too many, let's be clear, but that's a big reduction. The number of casualties on 20 mph and 30 mph combined is 23 per cent lower than in 2022, before the speed limit came into force.

Road casualty numbers fluctuate from year to year. It has always been acknowledged that this will take several years of monitoring and evaluation before firm conclusions can be drawn. That is the responsible position, but, equally, it is not accurate to suggest that the evidence demonstrates the policy is, and I use quotes, 'clearly not working'. The published data simply does not support that conclusion.

The same applies when looking at speeds and journey times. Transport for Wales has undertaken extensive monitoring on behalf of the Welsh Government. That monitoring has shown reductions in average vehicle speeds on roads affected by the policy. It has also shown that the impact on journey times is measured in seconds for many journeys, with journey times actually becoming more reliable

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Reform UK: Terfyn cyflymder diofyn 20 mya
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
actually becoming more reliable on 45 of the 60 roads monitored. Some drivers may experience very slightly longer journey times, and I understand that frustration but it is important that we deal with facts. 

We've heard repeated claims that the policy costs Wales £9 billion. That is not what the regulatory impact assessment says. The regulatory impact assessment applied standard UK transport appraisal methodology, which monetises changes in journey times. While this provides a useful measure of travel time impacts, it does not fully reflect the wider purpose of the policy. Adopting a broader conception of value, it is clear that a marginal increase in travel time is more than justified where it saves lives and improves safety, public health and quality of life. From that perspective, the primary question is not whether journey times are marginally longer, but whether Wales becomes a safer, healthier and better place in which to live for current and future generations. While the theoretical figures applied to travel time impacts are a commonly used tool, they do not and are incapable of reflecting the wider real impacts. The policy is intended to save lives and reduce injuries.

Compared to figures on 20 mph and 30 mph roads in England, casualties in Wales have reduced at a three times greater rate between 2022 and 2025. Whilst I and this Government stand over the fundamentals of this policy, I will also freely admit—and I think others will, even on the Labour benches—that there were issues with the implementation under our predecessors. And some of the points that Helen made earlier fall into that category. Plaid Cymru's proposal and a balanced and flexible approach to implementation were supported by a majority in the last Senedd; they could and should have been adopted from the outset. One of the clear lessons from implementation was that there were inconsistencies in how the policy was applied by councils across Wales, and that there were roads where local people felt that different speed limits would be more appropriate. Those concerns were heard, and as we've heard this afternoon, local authorities acted on those concerns.

The previous Welsh Government did eventually revise its guidance, clarifying criteria, working closely with local authorities and empowering highway authorities to review roads in light of local circumstances. Councils across Wales have reassessed sections of the network, engaged with communities, considered local evidence and, where appropriate, made changes. 

I'll make one final point, if I may. Some people wanted every road to remain at 20 mph; others wanted every road to revert to 30 mph. However, the feedback from local authorities was clear. When asked, their residents did not want their own road to return to 30 mph. We therefore want to continue with this more pragmatic approach: the right speed on the right road, informed by evidence and community engagement. I therefore urge Members this evening to vote on the amendment from the Government. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

Diolch, Lywydd. Those local authorities next year will be tested on that, if that's what the response was, because we'll be looking forward to taking this issue back out onto the doorstep and letting the people of Wales decide whether this was a good or bad policy.

This question here today for us was about honouring what was a manifesto commitment. We on these benches think it would be wrong to tell the public one thing and then stand up in this Chamber and say the complete opposite. A betrayal in trust of the electorate is an absolute disgrace, and we won't tolerate that. We are going to follow every manifesto commitment we did that put us in here. That's why we are discussing this.

The thing you failed to mention in your response there, Minister, was the people of Wales in this. You went through your figures, you spoke about those, but what about all those people who signed a petition to this place saying that it was wrong to do the roll-out, and 20 miles per hour doesn't work for them? We've heard the figure is 469,571—15 per cent of the people of Wales decided to take their time to sign a Senedd petition to try to send a clear signal to this place, and the problem was there were deaf ears in this place that didn't want to listen. Well, guess what? The people of Wales then sent these people here to these benches, so you will have to listen. That's what we are. [Interruption.] We're going in. It's coming.

Now, an opinion poll by the BBC in March showed

What? Oh, Minister, you've got more to say again now, have you? Is this the democracy of Plaid Cymru? Heckle from the front benches after having minutes of your own time. Trust me, I've got a lot to come to, Minister.

Diolch, Lywydd. As I was saying, we heard also from the benches opposite about how some councils hadn't reversed the decision, maybe because of the state that Labour left councils in with the lack of funds, they simply can't afford it. Some people don't want to put the burden on the taxpayer to undo your mistakes. That's the problem.

We can say that on these benches, but for people out there, time is money when they're on the roads. Actual people needing to get from one job to the next to pay their bills, to put food on the table. There is a real cost to this.

So, I think the remarks today—. Let's think of the bigger picture. I agree, road safety is an important issue, but there's a wider impact here. Even the last Welsh Government's assessment said that this policy could cost up to £4.5 billion in 30 years. That's a huge impact to the Welsh economy. Jobs going, livelihoods. How about we think of them when we're here? The people we represent. We in here, this Chamber, are servants to the people, not masters, where we get to ignore them. We don't get to turn our back when we don't like what the electorate are saying. It's important to listen, and that's why we are having what should be an important debate.

Now, you mentioned road safety to me earlier, Minister. We've addressed road safety. We've said that there are lots of things we could be doing and focusing our time on, where that money could have gone, from dangerous junctions to potholes galore. There is lots out there that we could be spending time on, but no, we have to be sitting here talking about this today, because a failed policy was rolled out.

And the fact that politicians don't accept it—and I agree with you, Janet, in your intervention. There's a reason that the Labour benches are so empty here today. Deaf ears should not be what the electorate get, and I do want to pay credit to you, Carmelo, for your contribution today, Jason, Helen, Janet,  for yours, and Gwyn, I do always enjoy it, like I said, but I don't know what the mobile phone—. I don't know how I could possibly get into that, I think that's a debate for another time at the end about spending more time outdoors. I urge Members today to vote on what they think their constituents would want. It's easy for some people to say, 'It doesn't have much of an impact, our lives aren't impacted by it.' My inbox and my colleagues' inboxes, and I'm sure yours, are impacted by people who are impacted by a policy that does have bad consequences. As we have said, we are not in here today saying that we want 30 mph or higher outside schools or hospitals, what we are saying is that roads that were safe before, that should be back to 30 mph, and to roll that out to councils so that they have to work backwards, not work forwards—. XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Cynnig NDM9305 Paul Davies

Cynnig bod y Senedd:

1. Yn nodi amcangyfrif Llywodraeth Cymru bod sector amddiffyn ac awyrofod Cymru gyda'i gilydd yn cyflogi 16,000 o bobl yn uniongyrchol, fod ganddo drosiant o £3.7 biliwn, ac yn cyfrannu tua £1.5 biliwn mewn gwerth ychwanegol gros i economi Cymru.

2. Yn cydnabod:

a) y cyfraniad sylweddol parhaus y mae'r sector amddiffyn yn ei wneud i Gymru;

b) pwysigrwydd sector amddiffyn ffyniannus ar adeg o ansicrwydd geowleidyddol; ac

c) bod gan Gymru hanes balch o gyfrannu at amddiffyn y Deyrnas Unedig.

3. Yn galw ar Lywodraeth Cymru i gefnogi'r sector amddiffyn drwy:

a) cyhoeddi strategaeth ddiwydiannol amddiffyn Cymru sy'n nodi sut i wneud y mwyaf o'r cyfleoedd economaidd, diwydiannol a sgiliau sy'n deillio o fwy o wariant amddiffyn y DU yng Nghymru;

b) cydweithio â darparwyr addysg bellach ac uwch i ehangu argaeledd prentisiaethau, addysg dechnegol a llwybrau graddedigion yn seiliedig ar anghenion y sector amddiffyn; ac

c) gweithio gyda Llywodraeth y DU i archwilio cyfleoedd i gryfhau buddsoddiad yn y sector amddiffyn yng Nghymru.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Motion NDM9305 Paul Davies

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Notes the Welsh Government's estimate that Wales's combined defence and aerospace sector directly employs 16,000 people, has a turnover of £3.7 billion, and contributes approximately £1.5 billion in gross value added to the Welsh economy.

2. Recognises:

a) the significant ongoing contribution that the defence sector makes to Wales;

b) the importance of a thriving defence sector at a time of geopolitical uncertainty; and

c) that Wales has a proud history of contributing to the defence of the United Kingdom.

3. Calls on the Welsh Government to support the defence sector by:

a) publishing a Welsh defence industrial strategy setting out how to maximise the economic, industrial and skills opportunities arising from increased UK defence spending in Wales;

b) collaborating with further and higher education providers to expand the availability of apprenticeships, technical education and graduate pathways based on the needs of the defence sector; and

c) working with the UK Government to explore opportunities to strengthen investment in the defence sector in Wales.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig: Y sector amddiffyn
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Motion moved.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig: Y sector amddiffyn
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Lywydd. I move the motion on the order paper in the name of my colleague, Paul Davies. 

Those of us who remember the cold war remember living under the shadow of a potential nuclear conflict. I can vividly remember being glued to the telly as we watched the spectacle in our house of the Berlin wall coming down back in 1989, followed by the ripping back of the iron curtain as the communist regimes across eastern Europe began to collapse, the declarations of independence in the Baltic states and then the dissolution of the Soviet Union. It gave us all a great sense of hope, optimism for the future. The arms race was over and we all felt that it would be an end to the threat of war, particularly on the continent of Europe. But as we all know now, unfortunately, it has not been so.

Russia's invasion of Ukraine has brought war back onto our doorstep in Europe, and we know that there are hostile states across the world who threaten our national security. Only this weekend, we saw counter-terrorism police scrambling to RAF Fairford and making those arrests on the suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. That investigation, of course, is ongoing. And I know that everybody in this Chamber will join me in condemning any attempt to attack an RAF base or any other military base in Britain, in spite, actually, of the history of some political parties in this Chamber.

In a few weeks, we are going to remember those heroes who sacrificed so much for the freedoms we all enjoy in our country today. But bravery alone cannot stop a missile, it can't protect a ship and it can't keep a pilot alive when an aircraft fails. Our armed forces need and deserve the very best equipment that we can provide them. And those who make that equipment and the technology that it requires are also just as critical to our national security as those on our front lines in the military. We saw on Anglesey last week, didn't we, the fact that two RAF crewmen survived after ejecting from a Hawk aircraft near RAF Valley. And behind that moment of survival was a Welsh defence manufacturing company, because the pilots owe their lives to the parachutes made by Bridgend-based IrvinGQ, which were attached to the ejector seats that catapulted them out of that aircraft just before it crashed. So, our defence sector is vitally important. It is critical to our nation and our national security, especially at times like this.

Now the previous Welsh Government estimated that the aerospace and defence sector across Wales employed around 16,000 people. I see that there's been a revision upwards in that figure, which obviously I really do welcome.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig: Y sector amddiffyn
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
which obviously I really do welcome.

And my message, and our message, as a Senedd to those individuals, those workers in those industries today, should be very straightforward. It should be that we value what you do. We will champion your role in our defence and security as a nation, and we value your role in our economic security too. My party seeks to support opportunities to attract further defence-related investment to Wales, and I had hoped that all political parties in this Senedd could be united and agree on these particular issues. But I have to say, having seen some of the announcements and actions of the Welsh Government in recent weeks, and the unnecessary amendment to our debate today, I'm now not so sure as to where the Welsh Government stands on this issue, particularly that announcement on pausing investment in our defence industry in order that you can undertake this ethical defence review. I think that that is a recipe for disaster. It sends absolutely the wrong signal to those businesses that are getting ready to invest in different parts of the UK as the spending taps come on, because we need to make sure that we spend more on defence as a nation. And yet, at the very same time those businesses are trying to make decisions about where to invest, the Welsh Government puts on the brakes and says, 'Stop, we're going to do a review.' It couldn't have come at a worse time. It couldn't have come at a worse time.

You seem happy, Cabinet Minister, for that investment to go elsewhere, and I'm looking forward to your contribution to this debate today, because you need to put on record that Wales is open for this investment in order that we can secure those important jobs in our defence industry and create new, highly paid, well-skilled jobs in the future as well. And I think what you need to tell us is how long is this pause on investment going to be. How long are companies going to have to wait before they get a signal from you that Wales is still open for business? How many projects have been affected by that pause so far? How many millions have been set to one side as a result of this pause? What new tests are you expecting to apply to firms that are already operating under an ethical framework effectively within the UK, and legally operating and producing things, some of which are being exported? Are you going to be judging, as a Government, on whether an ejector seat or a parachute that's going to be strapped to an RAF jet is an ethical choice or not? I think it's very bizarre. It's baffling, and I'm concerned about it. Investors need certainty. Workers need certainty, but you're creating uncertainty, and that's bad for business. It's not good for business at all.

You say, or appear to say, that you value defence jobs, and yet you are deferring decisions that could be supporting those defence jobs and making sure that we attract them. Just last year, prior to the Senedd elections, I challenged the Development Bank of Wales on a restriction on arms manufacturing investment in this Chamber. It's only after I pressed them on that issue that the bank publicly clarified that that exclusion had been removed. Defence firms need plain answers. They don't need uncertainty. And I'm afraid that your amendment replaces our very clear call for a Welsh defence industrial strategy with just warm words about jobs and a request for us to endorse an ethical framework that hasn't even been published. We don't know who is undertaking the review. You haven't told us which individuals you're going to be listening to, and whether there's any involvement of the defence sector itself in that review or any engagement with them. These are important things, and I think we need to know as a Chamber—the nation needs to know—where you stand on this issue of defence. What are you going to do to help grow the industry here in Wales?

In July, the economy and enterprise Minister, to be fair, went to the Farnborough airshow. Very pleased to see you go there, and I know that you met with some defence companies while there. I commend you for doing that, but I was really disappointed that when those businesses came to Newport, when they came to Newport just down the road, you chose not to meet them. Even though you were down to be a speaker at that event, you didn't turn up. What sort of message does that send to these big multinational corporations that might want to invest in Wales? I'll tell you what message it sends. It sends a message, 'We don't want you here,' and I'm afraid that's absolutely the wrong message that you should be sending, especially given the value of the defence industry to our country and the value of it to our economic and, obviously, national security.

So, businesses deserve an answer. We don't need more stalling. We don't need you holding up

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig: Y sector amddiffyn
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: We don't need you holding up the creation of well-paid jobs and investment. Instead of sending out these mixed signals and these mixed messages to those businesses that are waiting to make decisions on where they invest, I think everybody in this Chamber should reflect, you should back our motion, you should demonstrate to those businesses and those workers in the defence industry across our country, who do so much to contribute to our national security, that you are on their side. You should make sure that we express, as a Senedd, a welcome in the increased defence spending by the UK Government, and every one of us in this Chamber should be fighting for Wales to get our fair share. You often talk about the fair share of investment on rail, right? And I'm all for that as well. But let's get our fair share of defence investment into Wales as well. That's why you need to get behind this motion. Let's develop that strategy to grow our defence sector. Let's try to boost the opportunities that that brings to our economy, our advanced manufacturing centre, our education providers, opportunities for research and development right at the cutting edge that, of course, can help to transform other parts of our economy too. It's the duty of every single Government, including every single Government in the United Kingdom, to keep our citizens safe and secure. Wales should play its full part in ensuring that we have an armed forces that are equipped with the modern capabilities that they need to be able to do just that. So let's back them, back our defence sector. I urge Members to support the motion.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Amendment 1—Heledd Fychan

Delete all and replace with:

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Notes the most recent industry estimate that Wales's combined aerospace, defence, security and space sectors directly employ 18,500 people, has a turnover of £5 billion, and contributes approximately £2 billion in gross value added to the Welsh economy.

2. Recognises the contribution of the defence sector to jobs, skills, innovation and productivity growth in Wales.

3. Supports the development of an ethical defence investment framework.

4. Welcomes that the framework will be underpinned by the Welsh Government’s commitment to international solidarity, respect for human rights and the rule of international law.

5. Notes the Welsh Government will continue engagement with industry, trade unions, the peace movement and other stakeholders as the framework is developed and reviewed over time.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig: Y sector amddiffyn
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch. Here in Cymru, we had a proud tradition of peace activism. Many of us can trace our family history back to a woman who signed the Welsh women's peace petition. St Fagans held a powerful exhibition tracing that journey from the women who organised for peace in the aftermath of the first world war to the women of Greenham Common who sacrificed so much in their campaign against nuclear weapons. Once again, we find ourselves living through turbulent times with devastating conflicts unfolding across the world. And, of course, there remains a pragmatic need for defence, and we must engage honestly with that reality.

I welcome the work that this Plaid Cymru Government is undertaking to develop an ethical defence investment framework. It presents a real opportunity to build on the Scottish Government's human rights due diligence approach, which evaluates businesses before they receive public grants or investment, and to establish a gold standard for ethical investment here in Wales. This framework is the first of its kind in Cymru, and Wales can be world-leading in setting clear expectations that public money should never support companies linked to human rights abuses or violations of international law. It allows us to stand on the shoulders of those women who came before us and carry forward their commitment to peace, justice and ethical leadership. Whether the conflict is in Gaza, South Sudan or Ukraine, we should be clear in our determination that no weapon manufactured, even in part, in Wales should ever be used in a way that breaches international human rights law.

Global responsibility is not just about following money. It is about ensuring Wales is never complicit in human rights abuses, and that our economic choices reflect our commitment to peace, justice and international solidarity. But we must also be honest about the wider questions this debate raises. Defence spending is often presented as an economic opportunity, but what kind of economy do we want to build here in Wales? The people of Wales elected this Plaid Cymru Government with a mandate for a different kind of economy, an economy that places our people and communities at its heart. They voted for an economic model rooted in ownership and community wealth, ensuring that wealth generated in Wales remains in Wales, building stronger communities, creating opportunity and delivering prosperity that is shared by all. If that is our ambition, then we must also ask who owns Wales's arms and defence manufacturing facilities and whose interests they serve. In many cases, ownership rests with large multinational corporations and private firms whose primary responsibility is to shareholders—

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig: Y sector amddiffyn
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig: Y sector amddiffyn
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
No, I won't. 

Rather than to communities in which they operate. When we talk about wealth leaking from Wales, this is exactly what we mean. Wealth created by Welsh workers and Welsh communities flowing out of Wales, rather than being reinvested in the places that need it most. That also raises questions about who gets to make decisions with profound consequences for peace, security and human rights.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig: Y sector amddiffyn
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
others are prohibited because of their effects. With weapon systems, how they are deployed and used matters enormously. The UK's export licensing criteria already address the risk of equipment being used to commit or facilitate serious violations of international humanitarian law. Welsh Ministers need to explain what their framework will add and why that benefit justifies any further bureaucracy, administration and expense. Delays could encourage businesses to invest elsewhere.

I can't say this framework hasn't already cost Welsh jobs. I can demand that Ministers assess the risk on investment and employment. Welsh workers deserve to know that their livelihoods are being properly considered. I want Wales to play a confident part in a strong United Kingdom, with skilled people making equipment we can rely on and businesses capable of competing for work. I want this motion to lead to apprenticeships someone can apply for, a contract a Welsh business can bid for and a stronger Welsh defence industry. Deliver the training, help firms win contracts and give investors clear answers.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig: Y sector amddiffyn
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
There's a somewhat irony here that only last week, when we were scrutinising and challenging your ethical defence framework, the aircraft went down at RAF Valley. I would hope that everybody on these benches are glad that those two pilots were able to eject and that they're well now after receiving treatment for minor injuries. I'm incredibly proud of that base. I'm also incredibly proud of the defence industry across Wales and the United Kingdom. And I'm incredibly proud also of those who serve, and have served previously, in our armed forces. Those who have lost their lives so that we have the freedom of speech here in this place. Now, I've enjoyed so many excellent contributions today, bar one. I will leave it at that.

It should be noted that the ejection seats in that aircraft were made by Martin-Baker, a company based in Denham. The company's own data notes that these seats have saved almost 8,000 aircrew lives around the world, but it is shocking to note that this essential business has been subjected to vandalism and factory occupation by Palestine activists simply because the Israeli Air Force utilise their ejection seats. This type of behaviour should be firmly reprimanded and these essential companies should be protected.

This crash last week served rightly as a reminder to us all of the risks that each and every one of our brave servicemen and women take in protecting our country. And when I say 'our country', I mean the United Kingdom to include Wales. Our vital defence sector uses a wide range of high-value skills that makes it naturally an ideal partner for schools, colleges and universities. It also employs over 18,500 people, has a turnover of more than £5 billion and contributes around £2 billion of gross value added to the Welsh economy. This industry contributes significantly to both our Welsh economy and our nation's safety. It provides highly skilled employment, supports supply chains across Wales and creates opportunities for collaboration between industry and our education. And following the crash last week, when I got out of this Senedd, even though I had to go on somewhere, I made a point of contacting RAF Valley, sending them my best wishes and assuring them of our 100 per cent support.

Now, unlike the Welsh Government, some within Plaid Cymru in particular want to move the arms industry out of Wales due to what they describe as a feeling of complicity in death.
